question: Your vehicle breaks down on a road (not a motorway). How far behind it should you place a warning triangle?
options: At least 100 metres
At least 25 metres
At least 45 metres (147 feet)
At least 10 metres
explanation: If your vehicle breaks down, think first of all other road users and get your vehicle off the road if possible. Warn other traffic by using your hazard warning lights if your vehicle is causing an obstruction. Put a warning triangle on the road at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your broken-down vehicle on the same side of the road, but never use them on motorways. Keep your sidelights on if it is dark or visibility is poor. (Highway Code rule 275.)

question: Where should you NEVER use a warning triangle?
options: On a single carriageway
On a dual carriageway
On a motorway
On a road with a 30 mph limit
explanation: If your vehicle breaks down, think first of all other road users and get your vehicle off the road if possible. Warn other traffic by using your hazard warning lights if your vehicle is causing an obstruction. Put a warning triangle on the road at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your broken-down vehicle on the same side of the road, but never use them on motorways. Keep your sidelights on if it is dark or visibility is poor. (Highway Code rule 275.)

question: Your car develops a fault on a motorway and you stop on the hard shoulder. How should you position the vehicle?
options: Straddling the rumble strip so other drivers see you
In the centre of the hard shoulder
With the wheels turned to the right
As far to the left as possible with the wheels turned to the left
explanation: Additional rules for motorways. If your vehicle develops a problem, leave the motorway at the next exit or pull into a service area. If you cannot, you should pull onto the hard shoulder and stop as far to the left as possible, with your wheels turned to the left. Switch on your hazard warning lights. (Highway Code rule 276.)

question: After stopping on a motorway hard shoulder, what should you and your passengers do?
options: Stand in front of the vehicle to warn traffic
Leave the vehicle by the doors furthest from traffic and wait behind the safety barrier
Stay in the vehicle with seat belts on
Attempt repairs at the rear of the vehicle
explanation: Keep well away from your vehicle and moving traffic. If you are able, exit your vehicle by the door furthest from traffic. Get behind a safety barrier where there is one. Do not stand in a place where your vehicle could be pushed into you if hit. Do not attempt repairs on your vehicle while it is in a live traffic lane or on the hard shoulder. (Highway Code rule 277.)

question: Something falls from your vehicle onto a motorway. What should you do?
options: Pull into a place of relative safety and contact the emergency services — do not retrieve it yourself
Stop in the lane and pick it up quickly
Reverse along the hard shoulder to it
Leave it — other drivers will avoid it
explanation: If anything falls from your vehicle (or any other vehicle) onto the road, only stop to retrieve it if it is safe to do so. On a motorway, do not try to remove the obstruction yourself; pull into a place of relative safety and contact the emergency services. (Highway Code rule 280.)

question: You stop to help at a road traffic incident. What is one of the first things you should do?
options: Clear the wreckage off the road
Move casualties out of vehicles immediately
Give casualties something warm to drink
Switch off vehicle engines and make sure no one is smoking
explanation: If you are involved in an incident or stop to give assistance, if possible stop in a place of relative safety, use your hazard warning lights to warn other traffic, put on high-visibility clothing if you have it, ask drivers to switch off their engines and stop smoking, and arrange for the emergency services to be called immediately with full details of the incident location and any casualties (on a motorway use the emergency telephone which allows easy location by the emergency services). (Highway Code rule 283.)

question: You arrive at an incident involving a tanker displaying hazard warning plates. What should you do?
options: Open the tanker valves to relieve pressure
Try to rescue casualties from the cab
Keep well away, do not smoke and give the emergency services full details of the markings
Direct traffic past the scene
explanation: Incidents involving dangerous goods. If an incident involves a vehicle containing dangerous goods, switch off engines and DO NOT SMOKE, keep well away from the vehicle, do not be tempted to try to rescue casualties as you yourself could become one, call the emergency services and give as much information as possible about the labels and markings on the vehicle. (Highway Code rule 284.)

question: You are involved in a collision that causes damage to another vehicle. What MUST you do?
options: Drive on if no one is injured
Stop and give your name, address and registration number to anyone with reasonable grounds to require them
Report to your insurer within 14 days
Wait for the police to arrive before exchanging details
explanation: Documentation. If you are involved in a collision which causes damage or injury to any other person, vehicle, animal or property, you MUST stop. If required, give your own and the vehicle owner's name and address, and the registration number of the vehicle, to anyone having reasonable grounds for requiring them. (Highway Code rule 285.)

question: After a reportable collision you did not exchange details at the scene. Within what time MUST you report it to the police?
options: Only if someone was injured
Within 7 days
Within 48 hours
As soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours
explanation: If you do not give your name and address at the time of the collision, report it to the police as soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours. (Highway Code rule 286.)

question: Your engine catches fire. What should you do?
options: Drive to the nearest garage
Pour water onto the bonnet
Get everyone out and away from the vehicle and call the fire brigade — do not open the bonnet
Open the bonnet and use a fire extinguisher
explanation: If your vehicle catches fire, get everyone out of the vehicle quickly and to a safe place. Do not attempt to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment, as opening the bonnet will make the fire flare. Call the fire brigade. (Highway Code rule 287.)

question: Your vehicle stalls on a level crossing and the warning bells start to ring. What should you do FIRST?
options: Get yourself and any passengers out and clear of the crossing
Push the vehicle clear
Phone the signal operator
Try to restart the engine
explanation: If your vehicle breaks down on a level crossing, or if you stall, get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing immediately. Use a railway telephone if available to tell the signal operator. Move the vehicle clear of the crossing only if there is time before a train arrives. If the alarm sounds, or the amber light comes on, leave the vehicle and get clear of the crossing immediately. (Highway Code rule 299.)

question: A casualty at a collision has a burn. For at least how long should you cool it with cool water?
options: At least 10 minutes
At least 30 seconds
At least 20 minutes
At least 5 minutes
explanation: At least 20 minutes. Source: The Highway Code, Annex 7 (First aid on the road).

question: When checking whether an unconscious casualty is breathing, for how long should you look, listen and feel?
options: A single breath is enough
Up to 30 seconds
Up to 10 seconds
Up to 2 minutes
explanation: Up to 10 seconds. Source: The Highway Code, Annex 7 (First aid on the road).

question: A casualty is in shock after a collision. What should you do?
options: Keep them warm and reassure them — do not give them anything to eat or drink
Give them a warm sweet drink
Walk them around to keep blood flowing
Leave them alone to recover
explanation: Keep them warm and reassure them — do not give them anything to eat or drink. Source: The Highway Code, Annex 7 (First aid on the road).

question: In the DR ABC procedure, what does the “A” stand for?
options: Assess
Alert
Airway
Ambulance
explanation: Airway. Source: The Highway Code, Annex 7 (First aid on the road).

question: A motorcyclist is lying unconscious in the road after a collision. Unless it is essential, why should you NOT remove their helmet?
options: Removing it could worsen a neck or spinal injury
It is illegal to touch a casualty
It will make them colder
The helmet may be needed as evidence
explanation: Removing it could worsen a neck or spinal injury. Source: The Highway Code, Annex 7 (First aid on the road).
